Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Vitamin D plus probiotic co-supplementation lowered Beck Depression Inventory scores compared with placebo in women with PCOS.
Sentence: "Vitamin D and probiotic co-supplementation, compared with the placebo, significantly improved beck depression inventory [β (difference in the mean of outcomes measures between treatment groups) - 0.58; 95% CI, - 1.15, - 0.02; P = 0.04], general health questionnaire scores (β - 0.93; 95% CI, - 1.78, - 0.08; P = 0.03) and depression, anxiety and stress scale scores (β - 0.90; 95% CI, - 1.67, - 0.13; P = 0.02)."
Measured as: beck depression inventory score
Population: Women with polycystic ovary syndrome aged 18-40 years
Intervention: 50,000 IU vitamin D every 2 weeks plus 8 × 10^9 CFU/day probiotic for 12 weeks
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 60
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not differ from placebo in seasonal affective symptom scores (SIGH-SAD) at 12 weeks.
Sentence: "There were no significant between-group differences in SIGH-SAD sums at 12 weeks (p = 0.7 (CI: - 3.27 to 4.81))."
Measured as: SIGH-SAD sum
Population: Healthcare professionals with seasonal affective symptoms (SPAQ-SAD question 2 score of 8 or more)
Intervention: 70 μg vitamin D daily for 3 months
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 50
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"evaluation":"All three call the pair genuine, which fits: both bear on vitamin D and depressive symptoms, the findings point different ways, and neither null is flagged as underpowered or pilot (B's CI is wide but the abstract doesn't say so). The question is the primary reason. Study A uses a combination product with probiotic (a co-treatment difference, under intervention) and a different dose and schedule, in PCOS women versus healthcare workers with seasonal affective symptoms. Population differs strongly (PCOS vs seasonal affective symptoms), but the probiotic co-treatment and dose difference are also strong; either is defensible. Response A picks population with a clear detail naming both population and co-supplement. Response B picks intervention and gives the most specific detail (dose and co-treatment figures), while listing population and outcome_measure as also differing. Response C picks intervention but is vaguer and attributes the explanation only to the probiotic. Since the rules explicitly note co-treatment as an intervention difference and B gives the most precise detail, B is slightly better than C; A is reasonable but population is somewhat less compelling given neither reports baseline status and the outcomes differ in kind.","ranking":["B","C","A"]}
